questions.question: Define pressure and give its unit. Use the particle model to explain how a gas exerts pressure and why the pressure acts equally in all directions.
questions.expected_answer: Pressure is the force acting per unit area: pressure = force ÷ area, measured in pascals (Pa = N/m²); 1 kPa = 1 000 Pa. Gas particles move rapidly and randomly in all directions and collide with the walls of the container; each collision exerts a tiny force, and the enormous number of collisions per second on each area of wall produces a steady force per unit area, the gas pressure. Because the motion is random, particles hit all walls equally often, so the pressure acts equally in all directions.

questions.question: Explain why a can full of steam is crushed when turned upside down in cold water, and how atmospheric pressure makes a drinking straw work. Why is atmospheric pressure lower in Johannesburg than at the coast?
questions.expected_answer: The cold water condenses the steam inside the can into a few drops of liquid, so very few gas particles remain inside and the inside pressure becomes very low. The air outside still exerts atmospheric pressure (about 101 kPa) on the outside of the can, so the much larger outside pressure crushes it. Sucking on a straw lowers the pressure inside the straw; atmospheric pressure on the surface of the drink is now greater and pushes the drink up the straw. Johannesburg is about 1 750 m above sea level, so there is less air above it pressing down and the air is less dense, giving fewer collisions; the pressure is about 83 kPa.

questions.question: State three ways to increase the pressure of a gas in a container and explain each with the particle model. Explain why aerosol cans carry a warning not to leave them in the sun.
questions.expected_answer: 1) Add more particles (e.g. pumping a tyre): more particles in the same volume, more collisions with the walls per second, higher pressure. 2) Raise the temperature at constant volume: particles move faster, hit the walls more often and with more force, higher pressure. 3) Reduce the volume at constant temperature (e.g. pushing a blocked syringe): the same particles are crowded into less space, so they hit each area of wall more often; halving the volume doubles the pressure. In the sun the gas in an aerosol can heats up, its particles move faster and the pressure rises, possibly enough to burst the can.
